coredata.dc:description: In this work, graft copolymerization of n-butyl acrylate (BA) with methyl methacrylate (MMA) onto enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic cassava starch (CCS) was carried out in a semi-batch emulsion polymerization and the latexes were used as a binder for paper sizing agent. The purpose of this work was to substitute a portion of the BA/MMA by CCS (from 0 to 20 wt.%) in the copolymer and to investigate the consequent effects on the properties of the latex, films and coated paper (e.g., colloidal properties, cytotoxicity and water absorption). Cytotoxicity of polymer films, CCS and α-amylase was evaluated in human keratinocytes cells (HaCaT) for 24 and 96 h. The results show that the grafting efficiency decreased as the concentration of CCS increased. Nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analyses revealed successful grafting copolymerization of BA and MMA onto CCS. Polymer films and CCS solutions were not cytotoxic towards HaCaT cells until 24 h of incubation. Nevertheless, after 96 h of incubation, cell viability was below 70 %, which is an indication that the polymer films with 10 and 20 wt.% of CCS were cytotoxic after longer incubation times. The cell viability was lower as the concentration of CCS in the film increased. Water absorption of polymer films and coated paper showed a direct relationship with respect to both the content of CCS employed and the grafting efficiency. These results demonstrate the utility of enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic starch-graft-polymer as coating binders and as sizing agents for the paper and packing industry.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In this work, graft copolymerization of n-butyl acrylate (BA) with methyl methacrylate (MMA) onto enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic cassava starch (CCS) was carried out in a semi-batch emulsion polymerization and the latexes were used as a binder for paper sizing agent. The purpose of this work was to substitute a portion of the BA/MMA by CCS (from 0 to 20 wt.%) in the copolymer and to investigate the consequent effects on the properties of the latex, films and coated paper (e.g., colloidal properties, cytotoxicity and water absorption). Cytotoxicity of polymer films, CCS and α-amylase was evaluated in human keratinocytes cells (HaCaT) for 24 and 96 h. The results show that the grafting efficiency decreased as the concentration of CCS increased. Nuclear magnetic resonance (1H-NMR) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) analyses revealed successful grafting copolymerization of BA and MMA onto CCS. Polymer films and CCS solutions were not cytotoxic towards HaCaT cells until 24 h of incubation. Nevertheless, after 96 h of incubation, cell viability was below 70 %, which is an indication that the polymer films with 10 and 20 wt.% of CCS were cytotoxic after longer incubation times. The cell viability was lower as the concentration of CCS in the film increased. Water absorption of polymer films and coated paper showed a direct relationship with respect to both the content of CCS employed and the grafting efficiency. These results demonstrate the utility of enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic starch-graft-polymer as coating binders and as sizing agents for the paper and packing industry.

ce:section.ce:para: Cationic polymer latex nanoparticles are an important class of materials and have been widely employed in diverse applications in paper manufacturing for both wet-end and surface applications, cosmetics, food packing and biomedical applications as drug carriers [1–7]. In this sense, cationic starches are an alternative to produce cationic polymeric nanoparticles with a wide range of properties, such as positive charge, colloidal stability at low pH, porosity and printability for food packaging and paper coating applications [5,7–9]. Further, specific to the positive charge, one of the major advantages of cationic starch is their antimicrobial characteristic [2,4,6,8,9] and their applications for printing on paper, or printability [5].

Starch is one of the most abundant linear polysaccharides present in various plants and produced in large scale from rice, potato, cassava and corn [10,11]. It is biodegradable, biocompatible, non-toxic and hydrophilic, formed from anhydroglucose units, α(1–4) and α(1–6) glycosidic bonds [10,11]. The linear portion of starch, known as amylose, is composed mainly of α(1–4) linkages while the α(1–6) bonds give rise to a branched structure known as amylopectin. The ratio of α(1–4) linkages to α(1–6) linkages determines the type of starch and is responsible for specific properties like, water solubility and crystallinity [10,11]. Native starch has to be modified by chemical or physical methods to obtain the required properties for paper and food industry [7,10]. Cationic starches can be produced by reacting starch with compounds containing tertiary or quaternary ammonium, amino groups or cationic monomers, yielding a positive charge [10–12] and are available in the market in various grades, depending on their specific application [13].

Cationic starch and its derivatives have been employed extensively in the production of sustainable polymeric latex nanoparticles employing different vinyl monomers and initiators to produce renewable materials in paper coating as binders and sizing agents, with properties that combine the advantages of starch and synthetic polymer [7,8,14–18]. One of the main functions of cationic starch graft polymer latex in surface sizing is to improve paper strength and surface porosity for cost competitiveness, and to achieve better interaction between the cationic moieties of starch with negatively charged ink particles for improvements to printability [5,18,21,22]. On the other hand, the use of cationic starch as a coating binder is limited by its sensitivity to water. Previous studies have proven that starch-graft-copolymers have an advantage over the simple mixtures of synthetic latex or modified starch [5,7,8,17–19]. For this purpose, cationic starch needs to be modified chemically, enzymatically or physically to obtain reduced molar mass before monomer addition in order to improve the stability of polymer nanoparticles [8,14–23].

An industrial approach is based on the in-situ treatment of cationic starch by amylases for conversion of starches into oligosaccharides through the cleavage of glycosidic bonds [8,15–23]. Earlier investigations have shown that enzymatic treatment is a better method in preparing polymeric nanoparticles stabilized by starch for paper coating [8,15–20] over other grafting techniques. Brockmeyer, et al. [15] described the use of a α-amylase to cleavage of glycosidic bonds of starch with substitution degree of 0.045 mol mol−1 at 85 °C for 30 min. Cheng et al. [8,18–20] reported about degradation time of cassava starch by α-amylase at 80 °C and grafting efficiency in an emulsion polymerization of styrene, MMA and BA.

Normally the solid content in an industrial formulation of enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic starch to produce polymer latex for paper application is between 25 and 30 % due the limitations in viscosity and stability of the latex. The presence of starch-free, low degrees of grafting level, sensitivity to water and the use of enzymes can limit the viability of polymer latex for paper-coating applications [5,24,25]. In this sense, various drawbacks were still present, such as latex instability, cytotoxicity of polymer films and the presence of enzymes even in very small residual quantities. Therefore, it is desirable to understand the cytotoxicity of polymer films and CCS employed for paper application to reduce the amount of chemicals used in the paper industry and in surface treatment processes specifically.

Recently, Li et al. [24] reported that polymer latexes used in paper coatings may cause toxic effects in cells or organisms due the possible migration from paper packaging to food. For this reason, the cytotoxicity of cationic nanoparticles has been studied in this area for many risks to food contamination and other purposes [26]. However, given the industrial and scientific importance of polymeric nanoparticles stabilized by cationic starch for paper coating and the lack of reported data about the cytotoxicity of the polymer latex films, CCS and enzymes, an investigation into the CCS content was conducted.

In this work, the effect of enzymatic cationic starch on the properties of starch-graft-poly(n-butyl acrylate-co-methyl methacrylate) latexes and films, produced by surfactant-free emulsion polymerization was studied. The purpose of this work was to understand the effect of enzymatically degraded CCS content (from 0 up to 20 wt.%) on the colloidal properties of the latexes and on the cytotoxicity of polymer latex films in human keratinocytes cells (HaCaT) for 24 and 96 h. Cytotoxicity information is helpful for industrial application, such as paper coating to predict the cytotoxic effect of newly developed materials. Poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) latexes were employed as sizing agents for paper, and the surface wettability was evaluated by Cobb60, Hercules sizing test and contact angle analysis. This work was developed in collaboration with BASF S.A., as an effective strategy for the use of starch-graft-polymer as binders and sizing agents for the paper and packing industry.

Methyl methacrylate (MMA) and n-butyl acrylate (BA) were supplied by BASF SA (Brazil) and were washed with NaOH solution (2.5 wt.%) to remove any traces of inhibitor and stored at −4 °C prior to use. Ferrous ammonium sulfate hexahydrate was obtained from Millipore-Sigma and hydrogen peroxide (HPO, 35 %) was obtained from Acros Organics. Cationic cassava starch (CCS, Amylofax® T15) was provided by Avebe, purified by washing with ethanol several times and then dried in an air circulation oven at 50 °C for 24 h before use. Thermostable α-amylase enzyme (α-1,4-glucan-4-glucanohydrolase) from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens with activity of 120 KNU-B/g (Aquazym® 120 L) was obtained from Novozymes Latin America Ltd. (Brazil). Alkyldiphenyl oxide disulfonate (Dowfax 2A-1, Dow Chem., 45 % active phase) was used as anionic surfactant to prepare the control sample. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.9 %), chloroform (CHCl3, 99.8 %) and 3-(4,5-Dimethyl-2-thiazolyl)-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide (MTT) were purchased from Millipore-Sigma. Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH = 7.4), Dulbecco’s modified eagle medium (DMEM) and fetal bovine serum (FBS) were obtained from Gibco™. Ethanol (EOH, 99.8 %), calcium acetate (99.8 %) and acetic acid were obtained from Lab. Synth. Deuterated dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO-d6, 99.9 %) and chloroform-d6 (99.9 %) were purchased from Millipore-Sigma. Deionized water with a conductivity of 2.3 μS cm−1 was used throughout the study.

Viscosity of CCS aqueous solution at 20 wt.% was determined at 50 °C using a Brookfield viscometer with spindle R1 at 60 rpm. After purification, CCS aqueous solution was prepared in deionized water at 85 °C under magnetic stirring and then cooled to 50 °C before analysis. The pH of CCS solution was measured using a digital pH meter (Orion model 310) at 25 °C.

The CCS was purified by washing with ethanol, neutralized with 0.1 M HCl solution, filtered under vacuum and dried in an oven at 40 °C for 24 h. Three samples were dissolved and titrated with 0.1 M NaOH on phenolphthalein as indicator. Degree of substitution was determined in triplicate using following Kjeldahl Method and was calculated using the following Eq. (1) [12,27,28].

The 1H NMR spectrum of CCS was acquired on a Varian Oxford spectrometer, operating at a field frequency of 300 MHz and 32 scans. After purification, CCS (6 mg) was dissolved in 0.6 mL of DMSO-d6, followed by heating the mixture at 40 °C for 30 min. The DS is also obtained using the relation described by Gaborieau et al. [23].

Elemental analysis of CCS was performed on a Leco CHN 628 elemental analyzer to determine carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen. The samples were first purified by washing with ethanol and dried in an oven at 50 °C overnight prior to analysis under argon carrier gas.

) of CCS was measured by using a gel permeation chromatography (GPC, Waters) equipped with Waters 1515 HPLC pump, Waters 2414 RI detector and Waters Ultrahydrogel 120 and 500 columns (7.8 × 300 mm) with either in the solvent mixture of HPLC H2O/ethanol/acetic acid with 0.5 M sodium acetate at a flow rate of 1.0 mL min−1 at 40 °C. CCS sample was dissolved in water bath at 80 °C for 30 min. and then was filtered through a 0.45 μm pore-size polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) syringe filter. The molar masses and the dispersity index values were derived from a calibration curve based on narrow poly(ethylene oxide) standards.

All polymerizations were carried out using different amounts of CCS in a 0.6 L jacketed glass reactor, equipped with a sealed mechanical stirring implement, condenser, thermocouple, temperature controller and nitrogen purging tube. The synthesis was carried out by semi-batch emulsion polymerization in a two-step process for various ratios of CCS. In the first step, the reactor was initially loaded with the CCS (0–100 g, dry basis) dispersed in deionized water (215 g), calcium acetate (0.15 g) and α-amylase enzyme (0.04 wt.% based on the dry starch). The mixture was heated at 85 °C with constant stirring (180 rpm). When the temperature reached at (85 ± 2) °C the mixture was maintained by 15 min. Immediately after, the α-amylase enzyme was inactivated by adjusting the pH with glacial acetic acid (6.5 g). This step was carried out in the same reactor in which the polymerization was conducted. The CCS-7* latex was produced with CCS that was not enzymatically treated, while the CCS-0 was produced without CCS using an anionic surfactant (7.0 g). In the second step, ferrous ammonium sulphate solution (0.28 g) in deionized water (5.0 g) and was loaded into reactor. After, HPO solution (0.7 g) in deionized water (10 g) was added every 5 min. using a dropping funnel. The monomer mixture (MMA/BA) and HPO solution (70.0 g) at 2.5 % v/v were added dropwise feed rate over a period of 3 and 4 h, respectively. In all runs, HPO concentration in the feed was kept constant. The internal temperature of the reactor was set to (85 ± 2) °C and maintained for 30 min. Finally, the polymerization was cooled to 30 °C, and was then filtered using a 60 μm nylon screen. All polymerizations were performed with BA/MMA ratio of 55/45 by weight. Table 1 shows the recipes used to prepare the starch graft polymer nanoparticles.

Overall conversion was determined by means of gravimetric analysis. The polymerization was interrupted by using a hydroquinone solution in combination with an ice-water bath and aliquots were put in pre-weighed aluminum pan and dried in an air circulation oven for 1 h at 140 °C. Each analysis was repeated three times and the average values were reported.

The latexes were characterized in terms of intensity-average hydrodynamic diameters and hydrodynamic diameter distribution (HDD) using a Delsa Nano C, Beckman dynamic light scattering (DLS) at 25 °C using Stokes-Einstein equation. Samples were filtered, diluted in deionized water and then approximately 2 mL was put into a quartz cuvette and then measured by DLS. This procedure was repeated three times with a new sample. The stability of the polymer nanoparticles was also determined in terms of average hydrodynamic diameter and hydrodynamic diameter distribution after storage in an air circulation oven for 72 h at 60 °C. The viscosity was determined at 20 °C using a Brookfield viscometer with spindle R1 at 60 rpm.

Zeta potential measurements were obtained in aqueous media on a Beckman Coulter, Delsa Nano C instrument, calibrated with NaCl solution (0.1 M). The latexes were diluted in water and measured at 25 °C. Results are presented as average of three measurements. The pH of the latexes was adjusted with ammonium hydroxide solution (5 % v/v) and then was measured on an Orion model 310 digital pH meter at 25 °C. The samples were analyzed in triplicate at 25 °C and all values presented are the average of three measurements.

The concentration of coagulum in the latex after polymerization was determined by gravimetric analysis using a stainless-steel screen (125 μm). A sample of 100 g of latex was diluted with 500 g water, filtered through a stainless-steel screen and then dried in an air circulation oven for 1 h at 110 °C. After drying, the mesh and retained material were weighed and the concentration of coagulum was determined [29]. The coagulum content is expressed as parts per million based on the original mass of latex sample.

Morphological characterization of polymeric nanoparticles and the location of the polymer with respect to the CCS was carried out on a FEI TECNAI-12 transmission electron microscope (TEM) at an operating voltage of 120 kV. The latex samples were filtered using a 125 μm nylon screen, diluted with deionized water in a 1:200 and then a drop of dilute latex was placed on a coated 300-mesh copper grid and allowed to dry at ambient temperature for 24 h before analysis. The average diameter of the particles was measured using the image analysis software (Image J).

The water absorption of the polymer films was performed following the guidelines in the norm ASTM D 570 at (25 ± 2) ºC [30]. Polymer latex films were prepared in silicon molds at (25 ± 2) oC and (50 ± 5) % of relative humidity (RH) for 7 days. The dried films were weighed, placed in water for 5 h, removed from the water and weighted again. For all polymer films 10 samples were prepared (2.0 × 2.0 × 0.1) cm [31]. Surface tension of the polymer films and latexes was determined by means of the static contact angle and pendent drop methods, respectively at (23 ± 2)°C and (50 ± 5)% of RH, using a Krüss Drop Shape Analyzer (DAS 100). Calibration was performed with deionized water with surface tension of 72 dynes cm−1.

The cytotoxicity of CCS, α-amylase enzyme and polymeric films (CCS-0, CCS-10 and CCS-20) was evaluated in vitro by indirect method. Firstly, samples of polymeric films (0.17 g) were immersed in cell culture medium supplemented with fetal bovine serum (DMEM-10 % FBS) for 24 h and 96 h at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. Similarly, CCS and α-amylase were added to DMEM at different concentration and the final solution was incubated for 24 h and 96 h at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. Following, the DMEM was filtered in sterile filters (Millipore; 0.2 μm) and the final medium was named as samples extracts. Cells of human keratinocyte (HaCaT) cell line were cultivated at 37 °C and 5 % CO2 in DMEM-10 % FBS containing NaHCO3 (7 g L−1), streptomicine (0.1 g L−1) and ampicillin (0.025 g L−1). After reaching confluence, the cells were seeded into 96 wells plate at the concentration of 104 cells/well and incubated at 37 °C and 5 % CO2 for 24 h. Then, the culture medium was replaced by samples extracts and the cell viability was evaluated after 24 h and 96 h by MTT assay. After the incubation time, the samples extracts were withdrawn and the cells were washed with phosphate buffer saline (PBS). A solution of MTT (100 μL; 0.5 mg mL−1) and the cells were incubated for 3 h. The solution of MTT was replaced by DMSO in order to solubilize formazan crystals and the absorbance at 540 nm was measured in a plate reader (Biotek). The values of cell viability were calculated by considering the average of absorbance in the wells containing only cells with culture medium as 100 % of viability. All the assays were performed in triplicate.

After polymerization and filtration, the latexes were diluted to about 10 wt.% solids content and were purified by centrifugation using a Beckman, 64-R centrifuge at 20,000 rpm and 5 °C for 2 h. The solid precipitate was washed with deionized water several times and centrifuged again for 2 h to remove non-grafted CCS in the aqueous phase and any other impurities. The precipitate polymer was collected again, washed several times with a water/methanol mixture and then dried in an oven at 40 °C for 48 h [23,28]. In order to remove any non-grafted CCS and homopolymer, samples were washed with DMSO, filtered and then was dried at the same temperature in an oven for 48 h.

The FT-IR spectra of the graft copolymers and CCS after purification were recorded on a Shimadzu IR-Affinity 1 spectrometer at a resolution of 4 cm−1 in the frequency range 4000−400 cm−1 with resolution of 2 cm−1 by collecting 32 scans.

The presence of CCS grafted on the purified copolymers was confirmed by 1H NMR analysis using a Varian Oxford Spectrometer operating at a field frequency of 300 MHz and and 32 scans. Dimethyl sulfoxide (d6-DMSO) was used as solvent for poly(MMA/BA-g-CCS) and deuterated chloroform was used as the solvent for poly(MMA/BA) at 30 °C.

Graft copolymerization was determined in duplicate by Soxhlet extraction using chloroform as solvent. After purification, all polymer samples were dried in a vacuum oven at 40 °C for 12 h, weighted and kept for 20 h continuous extraction with chloroform. The insoluble polymer was dried in a circulation air oven at 60 °C until constant weight was achieved. The grafting percentage (GP) was then calculated as the ratio between the grafted copolymer after Soxhlet extraction (W2 ) and the weight of initial amount of dry CCS (W1 ) (Eq. 2) [18].

Differential scanning calorimetry was run on a DSC System HF (Mettler Toledo). After being purified, approximately 10 mg of polymer sample was enclosed in an aluminum pan and analyzed under N2 atmosphere at a flow rate of 30 mL min−1. The samples were heated from -20 to100 °C and cooled to -20 °C, and again heated to 150 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min-1.

The starch-graft-polymer latexes were used as binders for coated paper to improve the surface sizing effect. The surface sizing agent was prepared with different amounts of the polymer latexes without purification (4, 6 and 8 wt. %) based on dry starch. Firstly, cationic starch was dispersed in water (80 g L−1) at 70 °C for 20 min. Then, certain amount of the rheology modifier (0.1 wt. %) and graft polymer latexes were added into mixture and stirred for 15 min. Finally, the mixture was coated at one side 2.0 g m-2 on base paper sheets (85 g m-2) by a size-press machine. The coated sheets were then dried in an air circulation oven at 100 °C for 5 min and were conditioned at (25 ± 2) °C and (50 ± 5) % of RH for 7 days. All coated sheets were calendered with a speed of 2 m s−1 at 85 °C roller temperature and were subsequently conditioned for 7 days at (25 ± 2) °C and (50 ± 5) % of RH before characterization. The contact angle of paper was determined by means of the pendent drop at (23 ± 2) °C and (50 ± 5) % of RH, using a Krüss Drop Shape Analyzer (DAS 100). A 20 μL water drop was applied on the sample with a micro syringe and the contact angle was measured for 10 s in 1 s interval [32]. Calibration was performed with deionized water with surface tension of 72 dynes cm−1. This value measures the sizing efficiency of the surface agent and this value is an expression of the water absorption for paper in 10 s. The average value of ten measurements was also reported. Coob60 and Hercules size test (HST) were employed to measure surface wettability of paper [33,34]. This value measures the sizing efficiency of the surface agent and this value is an expression of the water absorption for paper in 60 s. HST was employed an aqueous penetrant solution (naphthol green B) in 2% formic acid (TAPPI-530 om-02) [34]. Five different positions for each coated paper were measured and the average values were reported.

In order to understand the parameters controlling the polymeric nanoparticles and extent of enzymatic degradation by α-amylase enzyme, the properties of CCS used in this work were determined and the results are summarized in Table 2 . It can be observed that the medium degree of substitution (DS) obtained by Kjeldahl’s method was 0.293 and the pH of aqueous solution at 30 % wt./v was 6.6. The results of DS obtained by elemental analysis and 1H NMR are also listed in Table 2 and are in agreement with the DS values obtained by Kjeldahl’s method. It has been found that there is a considerable percentage of nitrogen in the CCS, which can be accounted by the presence of amino groups in the backbone of starch. These results obtained are in agreement with the literature [12,13,27] and are higher than the values found for cationic starches available commercially [13]. Fig. 1 shows the 1H NMR spectrum of the cationic starch (CCS). When the glucose unit is substituted by amino groups in starch, the signal at 3.13 ppm associated with methyl protons bound to the nitrogen atom is present and the signals at 5.3 ppm for α(1–4) and at 5.2 and 4.6 ppm can be attributed to α and β reducing end, respectively (Fig. 1). The existence of these signals resulting from the hydrogen atom of the substituent indicates that a cationic group was introduced into the backbone of starch [23,35]. The viscosity of CCS solution is provided in Table 2 and the value obtained was 65 mPa.s at 50 °C. The weight-average molar mass (

of the cationic starches from different sources were between 105 and 106 g mol−1. However, the cationic starch employed in this study needs to be reduced in molar mass before using it as polymer stabilizer [8,18–20].

Fig. 2 shows the effect of the CCS content on the visual aspect of the graft polymer latexes. The enzymatic modification method was employed to obtain CCS fragments in the presence of hydrogen peroxide and ferrous sulfate as the redox initiating system. One can clearly see the change in color from white/grey (CCS-0) to brown with the addition of CCS, more specifically with 15 and 20 wt.% of CCS. For the polymer latex CCS-10, the change in color was intermediary, showing the effect of CCS on the aspect of the latexes. Hydrogen peroxide, ferrous sulfate and enzyme react with starch in the water to produce hydrolyzed compounds (dextrin, glucose and reducing substances), changing the coloration. On the other hand, the direct use of CCS (latex CCS-7*) resulted in low latex stability during the polymerization, evidenced by the formation of coagulum. In accordance with Cheng et al. [8], a short enzymatic degradation time of starch (<5 min.) results in unstable nanoparticles. Therefore, despite the use of HPO and ferrous sulfate, the CCS must be modified enzymatically to facilitate its incorporation into the latex particles up to a certain CCS concentration.

In this work, enzymatic hydrolysis times of 15 min. at (85 ± 2) oC resulted in a stable polymer latex and high overall conversion values were achieved in relative short time (4.5 h). Table 3 shows the effect of the concentration of CCS on the colloidal properties of the latexes after enzymatic treatment and polymerization. The results show that the final overall conversion is not dependent on the concentration of CCS, and that there is no correlation between the monomer and amount of CCS employed. The overall polymerization conversion without CCS was 98.7 % while that of the polymerization with 20 % CCS was 99.8 %. For polymerization conducted with 10 wt.% CCS, the overall conversion was 98.0 %, showing the same behaviour as the polymerization with no CCS. However, graft polymerizations performed with different amounts of CCS did not exhibit significant difference in the overall conversion when compared with the copolymerization carried out in the absence of CCS, whereas the use of CCS tended to decreased the average hydrodynamic diameter after 10 wt.% of CCS content. The hydrodynamic diameters (DH) increased from 127 nm (CCS-0) to 201 nm (CCS-7) and thereafter decreased to 112 nm (latex CCS-20). The hydrodynamic diameter distribution (HDD) of the latexes increased after 7 wt.% of CCS content and leads to a higher values of HDD. The HDD of CCS-7 latex was similar to CCS-0 latex synthesized with surfactant and narrower than that of those synthesized with 10, 15 and 20 wt.% of CCS. Cheng et al. [20] described that when the enzymatically hydrolyzed cassava starch concentration was increased from 8.3–16.6% in the polymerization of styrene with BA, the particle size decreased from 323 to 148 nm and the polydispersity index increased.

The surface tension values of the latexes (Table 3) were practically constant as a function of the concentration of CCS. The composition of the continuous phase, as well as the water solubility of the monomers and the polymer, affect the particle size and distribution due to the hydrophilicity and strong hydrogen-bonding potential of CCS [14]. However, the use of CCS after enzymatically hydrolysis showed themselves to be effective stabilizers that could be used as direct replacements for typical surfactants in emulsion polymerization to produce stable amphiphilic polymer particles with positive charge. Similar results were also reported for cassava starch by Cheng et al. [18,20].

Fig. 3 shows images obtained by TEM which reveal the spherical nature of the latex particles with CCS loadings of 0, 10 and 20 wt.% of CCS. The images show that polymer nanoparticles coverage by the CCS oligomers. For the latex CCS-0 synthesized without starch, the average particle diameter obtained by TEM is 113.6 nm (Fig. 3a), which is similar with the result of the hydrodynamic diameter measured by DLS (Table 3). The morphology of CCS-10 and CCS-20 with CCS around and between the polymer particles can be observed in Figure b–d, respectively. The average particle diameters measured for CCS-10 and CCS-20 (Fig. 3b–d) are 99.5 nm and 82 nm, respectively. These values are smaller than the results of the hydrodynamic diameter measured by DLS (Table 3) and can be explained by the presence of CCS either grafted or adsorbed on the polymer particles and by the fact that the particles were measured in the dry state, resulting in the particle deformation [20,23]. Similar results were reported by Cheng and Zhao [20].

The amount of coagulum (grit) expressed by as a fraction of the original latex mass increased as a function of the addition of CCS and this effect is more pronounced for latexes produced with 15 and 20 wt.% of CCS (Table 3). Coagulum contents at 79.0, 552 and 1385 ppm were obtained for 10, 15 and 20 wt.% of CCS, respectively. For the polymerization conducted without the addition of α-amylase (CCS-7*), we were unable to produce stable latexes, resulted in coagulation during the polymerization. This results may be due to the high molar mass of CCS before enzymatic hydrolysis (Table 2). Cheng and co-workers [19] reported similar results for non-degraded cassava starch in the emulsion copolymerization of styrene with BA. The coagulum is undesirable in many applications, particularly in paper coatings and must be prevented during the polymerization process. This result indicated that the enzymatic treatment promoted latex stability during polymerization due to the reduction in the average molar mass of the starch [23]. Normally, the presence of visible coagulum is an indicator that CCS was not fully grafted and that a significant amount remained in the aqueous phase. If a monomer is too hydrophilic it may cause excess water phase homopolymer formation. Later, when the liquid phase evaporated by coalescing the particles, CCS free on the surface of polymeric film can absorb more water.

The effect of CCS on the colloidal stability of latex is also confirmed by the results of the zeta potential (Table 3). When the CCS amount was increased, there was a corresponding decrease in the zeta potential from +20.4 mV (CCS-7), +19.5 mV (CCS-10) and +18.6 mV (CCS-15) to +9.3 mV (CCS-20) (Table 3). The zeta potential values may be related to the CCS molecules grafted at the surface of polymer particles acting as a stabilizer. In other words, the addition of CCS changed the zeta potential from negative (-47.3 mV) to positive with good colloidal stability. The zeta potential of the latex synthesized with surfactant (CCS-0) is -47.3 mV, which is very close in terms of hydrodynamic diameter. The values of pH were between 2.6–3.0 and provide direct evidence that CCS at pH between 2.6 and 3.0 has a stabilizing effect similar to that of emulsifiers, but with positive charge because of the amino groups in the CCS (Fig. 2). Thus, the addition of CCS after enzymatic treatment provide stability to the polymer nanoparticles during the polymerization and after 72 h at 60 °C in an oven (Table 3). The polymer latex has good storage stability and no coagulation appeared during the stability test. It can be concluded that the CCS molecules contribute to the stability of the nanoparticles by steric and electrostatic stabilization mechanism.

The effect of pH on the zeta potential of the latexes is shown in Fig. 4 . The zeta potential of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) latexes were positive at pH ≤ 3 and the values decreased with increasing pH. At pH 10 the zeta potential reversed, to being slightly negative for all latexes, due possibly to the screening effect of the positively charged CCS chains on the surface of the polymer particles. For the latex CCS-10, a distinct behaviour was seen, with lower values of zeta potential from +19.5 mV (pH = 3) to -27.7 mV at pH = 6 and -42.2 mV at pH = 10. At pH < 6, CCS is in the fully protonated form and positive charges are present on the surface of the polymer particles. It can be concluded that the sufficient amount of BA/MMA was grafted onto CSS (Fig. 5 c). For both latexes, the effective hydrodynamic diameters were practically constant, indicating good stability of the latexes within the pH range. When the pH of CCS-10 was increased from 3 to 10, the particles became more negativity due to deprotonation of amino groups grafted onto the polymer particles.

The FT-IR spectra of poly(BA/MMAA) and poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) with different amounts of CCS are shown in Fig. 6. The broad and strong peak at around 3300–3500 cm−1 is assigned to the stretching vibration of OH groups of CCS and the peaks at 1440, 1140 and 1017 cm–1 are attributed to the CO stretching vibrations of the glucose units [18,20,28]. The stretching vibration of methylene groups (C–H) is proved by the appearance of absorption peak at around 2950 cm−1 [20]. The peaks that appeared at 990 and 992 cm−1 were due to the stretching of the vinyl groups. A new peak at around 1025 cm−1 appeared after grafting of CCS and this band was not present in the CCS-0 spectrum and thus is an evidence for the presence of CCS on the backbone of the polymer. In the spectrum of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS), the absorption band at 1720 cm−1 is assigned to the CO vibration of MMA/BA and suggests that a certain amount of BA and MMA are grafted onto CCS [18,20]. The appearance of the new peaks in the spectrum of CCS-g-polymer provides substantial evidence that the MMA and BA were grafted onto CCS.

Table 4 shows the Tg and GP values for polymers produced with different amounts of hydrolyzed CCS (0−20 wt.%) which were analyzed after purification to separate the non-grafted CCS. The polymer produced without CCS was synthesized for reference in this work, under identical reaction conditions. The Tg of poly(BA/MMA) was approximately 8.0 °C, while the polymer with 20 wt. % CCS showed a small decrease in the Tg from 8.0–5.2 °C. This small decrease in Tg may be attributed to the graft percent (GP) of monomers to CCS backbone, especially BA (Tg ≈-54.0 °C) [41] and the presence of poly(MMA-g-CCS) in the water phase [19,40]. However, this decrease could also be attributed to BA present in the polymer backbone. The difference in reactivity ratios (rBA<rMMA) and the water solubility (MMA:12.25 g L−1 and BA: 1.65 g L−1) [41], would justify the tendency to form poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) richer in BA than in MMA [18]. The graft percent of CCS-7 was higher than that of CCA-10, CCS-15 and CCS-20 (Table 4). Therefore, at higher contents of CCS the Tg of the poly(CCS-g-MMA/BA) is improved greatly by the grafting percent of CCS (Table 4) monomer reactivity ratios. The estimated value of the Tg for the polymer without CCS using the Fox‐Flory equation is approximately 8.0 °C. However, comparing the values for CCS-7, the Tg values are similar to that of CCS-0. On the other hand, derivations from ideal values may occur between experimental and theoretical values caused by interactions between the CCS-g-polymer and free CCS in the water phase. These deviations give useful information about nucleation and graphitization mechanisms.

The solubility of poly(MMA/BA) and poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) after purification was analyzed in chloroform and the results are summarized in Table 4. The poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) became more resistant to chloroform with increasing CCS content into polymer. Significant change was observed when CCS loadings reached 20 wt.% (CCS-20). The difference observed as it relates to the amount of CCS employed (Table 1). The results suggest that 7 and 10 wt.% of CCS are the most appropriate for the grafting of MMA/BA by semi-batch emulsion polymerization for paper application because changes to the properties of the grafted polymers are minimized.

Cationic starch graft copolymers show the potential to improve the performance of paper coatings and have great potential in food packaging applications [24,25]. On the other hand, these kinds of polymer may have toxic effects on cells or organisms [24]. Thus, the cell viability of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) films containing 10 and 20 wt.% of CCS was evaluated by using HaCat cells and samples of the films. Cell viability was measured by MTT assay after the incubation of cells with samples extracts over different intervals of time. As shown in Fig. 7 b, we observed that polymer films extracts were not cytotoxic after 24 h since cell viability after 24 h was above 70 %. Thus, it can be stated that all the synthesized polymers are not cytotoxic as well as the standard polymer (CCS-0) after 24 h. However, after 96 h, cell viability of the polymers with CCS decreased. The cell viability was lower as the concentration of CCS in the film increased (Fig. 7b).

Cells incubated with extract of polymer films containing 10 % of CCS showed 59 % of viability whereas cell viability of cells incubated with the extract of polymer film containing 20 % of CCS was 38 %. Although these results could indicate the toxicity of CCS, when cells were incubated with CCS in solution at different concentrations no cytotoxicity of CCS was observed. The cell viability of cells incubated with CCS was above 80 % for all the concentrations. In a different study, Wang et al. [3] reported high cytotoxicity of spermine modified cationic starch against HepG2 cells. Cells incubated with cationic starch at a low concentration range (0.2–1.0 mg mL−1) showed cell viability lower than 60 %. Pereira et al. [36] reported that the cationic cassava starch was the most harmful sample tested with cells extracted from an African green monkey (VERO) after 72 h of incubation.

Herein, the cytotoxicity of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) films was proven to not be caused by the presence of CCS, since CCS was shown to be non-cytotoxic. Moreover, the cationic groups in the CCS backbone were non-cytotoxic to HaCaT cells at all concentration employed (Fig. 7a). Once the polymer films also contained α-amylase, cytotoxicity of this enzyme was also assessed by in vitro assays. At the concentration of 0.08 wt.%, cell viability was of 64 %, indicating cytotoxicity of the enzyme at this concentration (Fig. 7a). Taking into account that this concentration would be the same on average if all of the enzyme present in the films were released, the cytotoxicity of the films was attributed to the α-amylase. As showed in Fig. 8 , the absorption of water by films made with 20 wt. % CCS was greater than that of the films obtained with CCS. Out of all the enzymes, α-amylase is the key enzyme for starch depolymerization and polymer stabilization [7,8]. The enzyme α-amylase was used in the synthesis of the polymer (0.04 wt.% based on the dry starch) in order to obtain a CCS with low molar mass. In the synthesis, the enzyme was inactivated by lowering the pH of the medium, but it was not possible to remove it from the polymer films. Therefore, once the films were immersed into the cell culture medium where the pH was 7, the enzyme resumed its activity and may have compromised cell viability.

Fig. 8 shows the water absorption and surface tension of the poly(MMA/BA) and poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) films with different amounts of CCS. Significant changes in the absorption of water and surface tension were observed when CCS loadings reached 7 wt. % (Fig. 8). The polymer film without CCS showed low water absorption due to its high hydrophobicity and the polymer film with CCS showed poor water resistance due to the undesired polymer formation in the water phase during the polymerization step and grafting percentage of CCS. The contact angle exhibited a decreasing trend with the increase in CCS content. The films were produced without centrifugation of the latexes and, polymer films with non-grafted CCS resulted in more hydrophilic films. The results showed a clear trend in the water absorption and surface tension values as the starch-g-MMA/BA content increased. A positive aspect of these latexes was their low viscosity, good colloidal stability, lower particle size (< 300 nm), good film formation, and positive charge, which can result in good printability.

The absorption of water by films made with 20 wt. % CCS was greater than that of the films obtained with CCS concentrations of 7, 10 and 15 wt. %. The surface tension of the films was in agreement with the water absorption results and was dependent on CCS concentration. There was a significant difference from one concentration to another as determined by the Tukey test at the 0.05 level, which indicates that the means were significantly different. These results indicate that 7.0 wt. % CCS is the limit to maintain a level of resistance to water equivalent to that of the film generated from the latex without CCS. The difference in the surface tension above 7 wt. % CCS indicates that these nanoparticles display a higher affinity for the air water interface, which is associated with the amphiphilic characteristics of CCS chains. This may be an indication that the films were cytotoxic towards HaCaT cells after 24 and 96 h of incubation (Fig. 7b). The main point of interest is whether some of the CCS can be distributed at the film surface in sufficient concentration to significantly affect the contact angle. Starch, due to its hydrophilic nature, absorbs water through the formation of hydrophilic interactions with water molecules, mainly through the formation of hydrogen bonds [14]. However, the increasing CCS concentration and partial grafting of starch resulted in an increase in the sensitivity of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) compared to the non-grafted polymer. The difference observed in the absorption of water as a function of the addition of CCS can be linked to polymerization in the aqueous phase resulting in species with a greater affinity for water.

The effects of poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) latexes as surface sizing agents on the water resistance of paper (Cobb60 and HST) are shown in Fig. 9 and Table 5 , respectively. Fig. 9 gives a clear indication that papers sized with CCS-7 exhibited lower water absorption than papers sized with CCS-10 and CCS-15 for both latex concentrations employed. A larger reduction was observed for both papers sized, compared to the base paper. The base paper had a Cobb60 value of 173 g m−2 which was greatly reduced when sized with different amounts of CCS-7, CCS-10 and CCS-15. Increasing the latex concentration from 0 to 8 wt. % (CCS-7) on the base paper, decreased the Cobb60 value from 173 to 20 g m−2. The papers sized with CCS-15 gave a higher Cobb60 value than papers sized with CCS-7 for both latex concentration, which indicates a loss in hydrophobicity. The reason may be that the CCS-7 containing low amounts of CCS free in the water phase. The Cobb60 value shows the hydrophobicity of paper in contact with water for 60 s. These results are in good agreement with the HST results, indicating that the amount of BA/MMA grafted onto CCS could form a better hydrophobic layer on the surface of the paper compared to the un-sized paper (base paper). As a result, CCS-7 could improve the water resistance of paper through a higher grafting percentage, greater latex penetration into the interior of the paper and better film-formation, resulting in beneficial effects on the final film barrier properties [39].

As comparison, the Cobb60 value of the paper sized with CCS-0 synthesized with anionic surfactant exhibited lower water absorption than papers sized with CCS-g-polymers for both latex concentrations employed. The Cobb60 value decreased from 50 to 10 g m−2. The reason for that could be attributed to the formation of a hydrophobic layer on the surface of the paper sized with CCS-0. Thus, the starch grafted polymer had a significant effect on water resistance and HST values at the lower levels of addition of CCS and also at the highest levels of latex concentration (Table 5).

Contact angle vs. time of papers sized with different contents of CCS-7, CCS-10 and CCS-15 were also investigated, as shown in Fig. 10 a–c. As expected, water in contact with paper sized is absorbed rapidly and the contact angle increased as the amount of graft polymer onto CCS increases (Table 4). On the other hand, both results were better than base paper (unsized), suggesting the improvement of water resistance [37]. Papers sized with CCS-15 has the lowest contact angle compared to papers sized with CCS-10 and CCS-7. The contact angle values were more stable over time for concentrations between 6 and 8 wt.%. When the sample CCS-7 is compared with sample CCS-10 (6 and 8 wt.%), it can be seen that the contact angle over time for sample CCS-7 is much better than sample CCS-10. This is followed by CCS free in the water phase (not grafted), which resulted in less sized paper and demonstrated a tremendous increase in water absorbency of paper sized. This results are in agreement with water absorption and surface tension of the polymer films presented in Fig. 8. The penetration of water into paper depends basically on the penetration in the capillary system of the sheet, diffusion along the capillary and diffusion through the fibers [37,38]. Therefore, the presence of CCS free (not grafted) showed poor water resistance and decreased the sizing efficiency. This behavior may compromise the cell viability as showed in Fig. 7.

Stable cationic polymer latexes with different amounts of hydrolyzed cationic cassava starch (CCS) were successfully obtained by one-pot semi-batch emulsion polymerization. The latexes can be applied in several industrial applications including paper coatings. The grafting percentage decreased as the concentration of CCS increased. The optimal CCS concentrations that maximized not only particle size, but also water resistance and stability, were 7 and 10 wt.%, which are directly related to the efficiency of particle nucleation and grafting efficiency. After enzymatic hydrolysis, CCS acts as a colloidal stabilizer and small particles were obtained with lower amounts of CCS. The overall conversion was not affected by the amount of CCS employed. The coagulum concentration, surface tension and water resistance were influenced by the concentration of hydrolyzed CCS. The direct use of CCS without modification resulted in lower latex stability during the polymerization. Water absorption properties of polymer films and coated paper showed a direct relationship not only with the CCS content employed but also with the grafting efficiency. All relevant properties of the paper were improved when the poly(BA/MMA-g-CCS) latex was used as a binder. The polymer films and CCS solutions showed no cytotoxicity towards HaCaT cell. Nevertheless, the polymer films produced with 10 and 20 wt.% of CCS were cytotoxic after longer incubation times (96 h) after which the cell viability was below 70 %. The cell viability was lower as the concentration of CCS in the polymer increased. At the concentration of 0.08 % wt.%, cell viability of the α-amylase was of 64 %, indicating cytotoxicity at this concentration. The results presented in this work create a new approach for the application of enzymatically hydrolyzed cationic starch-graft-polymer latexes as coating binders and as sizing agents for the paper and packaging industry.
